summary: 2 Chronicles continues the history begun in 1 Chronicles. Chapters 1 to 9 deal with the reign of Solomon, almost entirely devoted to the building and dedication of the temple. After the division of the kingdom, the book follows only the kings of Judah, from Rehoboam to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians, and assesses each one by his faithfulness to God and his care for the temple. Reforming kings, such as Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah, receive a good deal of space. The book ends with the exile and with the decree of Cyrus, which authorizes the return to Jerusalem.
name: The Hebrew title, Divrei ha-Yamim, means “the events of the days,” that is, the annals. The Septuagint used the name Paraleipomena, “things left out,” and the name “Chronicles” comes from a suggestion of Jerome. In Hebrew tradition, 1 and 2 Chronicles form a single book; the division comes from the Septuagint.
facts: 14th book of the Bible, among the historical books; in the Hebrew Bible, the second half of the book of Chronicles, which generally closes the Writings (Ketuvim)

structure.title: Solomon and the temple
structure.text: The wisdom asked for at Gibeon, the building and dedication of the temple, the riches of the kingdom and the visit of the queen of Sheba.

structure.title: The division and the first kings of Judah
structure.text: Rehoboam, the separation of the northern tribes, Abijah and the long reign of Asa.

structure.title: Jehoshaphat
structure.text: Teaching of the law, alliance with Ahab, organization of justice and the victory over Moab and Ammon.

structure.title: From Jehoram to Ahaz
structure.text: A period of crises: the usurpation of Athaliah, the ambiguous reigns of Joash, Amaziah and Uzziah, and the idolatry of Ahaz.

structure.title: Hezekiah
structure.text: The purification of the temple, the great Passover and the deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib.

structure.title: From Manasseh to the exile
structure.text: Manasseh and his repentance, Josiah's reform, the last kings, the destruction of Jerusalem and the decree of Cyrus.

extra.title: Conduct and consequence
extra.text: More than Kings, the Chronicler links each king's destiny to his conduct in the same generation: faithfulness brings peace and victory, and forsaking God brings defeat or disease, as in Uzziah's leprosy (26:16–21). At the same time, the book insists on the possibility of turning back: only it tells that Manasseh, taken captive, humbled himself and was restored (33:12–13). Words such as “seek,” “humble oneself” and “forsake” appear often and help us read these stories.

writing.tradition: For the Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 15a), Ezra wrote the genealogies of Chronicles and Nehemiah completed the work. On this reading, the book would have been written in Jerusalem in the 5th century BC, around 450–400 BC.
writing.academic: 1 and 2 Chronicles are the work of the same anonymous author, called “the Chronicler,” linked to the circles of the temple in Jerusalem. The book uses Samuel and Kings as its main source and cites other records, such as those of prophets and seers (for example, 9:29; 33:19). Most scholars date it to the end of the Persian period or the beginning of the Hellenistic period, between c. 400 and 250 BC. The end of the book (36:22–23) repeats the beginning of Ezra; for a long time this was read as a sign of a common author, a hypothesis many now question.

events.intro: The book covers about four centuries, from the beginning of Solomon's reign, around 970 BC, to the decree of Cyrus, in 538 BC. The dates of the kings of Judah come from calculations based on the numbers of the text itself and on synchronisms with Assyrian and Babylonian records; different systems diverge by a few years, especially before the 8th century BC. Some episodes have outside confirmation: the campaign of Pharaoh Shishak (Sheshonq I) appears in a list of cities at Karnak, and Sennacherib's siege is narrated in the Assyrian annals.

context: Judah was a small kingdom, with its capital in Jerusalem, surrounded by larger powers: Egypt to the south, the Aramean kingdoms and the Northern Kingdom (Israel), then Assyria and, finally, Babylon, which destroyed the city in 587/586 BC. The author, however, writes for the community that returned from exile and lives under the Persians, with the temple already rebuilt. For this reason he reads the history of the kings from the standpoint of the temple and its worship and ends the book not with ruin but with the proclamation of Cyrus, which opens the way for the return.
note: Dates are approximate and vary according to the source. The BSB follows the numbering of English Bibles: in the Hebrew text, 2:1 corresponds to 1:18 and 2:2–18 to 2:1–17; 14:1 corresponds to 13:23 and 14:2–15 to 14:1–14. The verses quoted are from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).
